item.title: A $60 billion fintech hired a 14-year-old. Its CEO explains why.
item.description:
Ramp hired a 14-year-old intern after discovering an app he had built for fun that attracted attention from roughly a million people on Twitter.

Co-CEO Eric Glyman discussed the hire during a November 5 interview with founder and editor of Upstairs Media, Alex Konrad , explaining how the $60 billion fintech company evaluates engineering talent beyond traditional qualifications, a recalibration playing out across the industry as AI redraws what a junior role even means .

A viral app, no assignment

“We had an intern who was 14 years old,” Glyman said. “Part of how we found him was he had built his own app for fun that was genuinely useful, and a million people saw it on Twitter and interacted with it. There was no one who was telling him, ‘Hey, go build this project.’ He just was interested in it.”

Glyman did not identify the teenager or specify when he worked at Ramp.

“Part of how we found him was he had built his own app for fun that was genuinely useful, and a million people saw it on Twitter…”

The Minecraft server test

Glyman says Ramp looks for developers who have pursued projects on their own, even when that experience doesn’t come from a conventional job, a premium on self-direction that grows sharper as AI erodes the entry-level tasks that once trained new engineers .

“A lot of what we’re looking for is strong evidence that someone has built something on their own, created something on their own, and shown their drive where it didn’t come from other people saying, ‘I need you to go do something’.”

“A lot of what we’re looking for is strong evidence that someone has built something on their own… and shown their drive where it didn’t come from other people saying, ‘I need you to go do something’.”

In a separate November 3 interview with Blackstone , Glyman said Ramp also looks for developers who got their start running Minecraft servers as teenagers.

Some teens built their own servers before high school, gaining practical programming experience long before entering the workforce.

Glyman acknowledged that the approach has limits, since talented candidates who haven’t had the time, resources, or opportunity to build something independently could be overlooked at precisely the moment the entry-level rungs of the industry are already thinning out .

A 28-year-old running engineering

In June, Ramp appointed Rahul Sengottuvelu as chief technology officer at 28, replacing co-founder Karim Atiyeh , who became co-CEO alongside Glyman.

Sengottuvelu joined Ramp through a 2023 acquisition and later led its applied AI team. He was already building AI products before ChatGPT became a household name.

In its leadership announcement , Ramp pointed to Sengottuvelu’s experience building AI products and his ability to make tough technical decisions. He took over as CTO as the company was putting AI to work in more of its products and day-to-day operations.

Small teams own the call

Glyman also described how Ramp organizes its engineers into small teams of five or six people, giving them responsibility for deciding how to complete their projects.

“If you look really deep into Ramp’s organizational design, it’s tons of small teams where we say, ‘Here’s the outcome we want you to drive, but it’s up to you.’ You can make the call on how you want to spend your time. Why hire someone who can surprise you with their creativity and then tell them, ‘Don’t make your own recipe’?”

“Why hire someone who can surprise you with their creativity and then tell them, ‘Don’t make your own recipe’?”

Glyman says adding more engineers doesn’t always mean getting work done faster since bigger teams often mean more people weighing in on decisions, which can add churn and slow workflow.

Ramp instead gives smaller groups ownership of specific projects, with leadership setting the goals rather than prescribing every step.

For Glyman, hiring people capable of making their own decisions only makes sense if they’re allowed to do so once they’re on the job.

item.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 with a price cut and stronger coding scores
item.description:
On Monday, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 , the latest versions of its duo of flagship models.

Like before, Fable 5.2 will be available on all platforms today, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, while direct access to Mythos remains limited to organizations in Anthropic’s Cyber and Life Sciences verification programs.

Also like before, Fabe and Mythos share the same underlying model, but Fable ships with stricter cybersecurity and biology safeguards.

It’s maybe a bit of a surprise that Anthropic didn’t designate these models as “5.5,” given that its Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models are now at that version number.

The company stresses that it continues to recommend that users go with Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, while Fable 5.2 is meant to help users “tackle the most daunting technical challenges.”

And while both models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, according to Anthropic, one feature the company is stressing here is speed. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, the company says, generate output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, respectively.

Fable Fast mode

For those who want an even faster response, there is now also a Fast mode for both models, which Anthropic says speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times.

It is available in Claude Code, on the Claude Platform, through Claude Models on Google Cloud, and through Anthropic-hosted Microsoft Foundry.

Pricing

As for pricing, Fable still carries a premium over Opus, but Anthropic is cutting the price from $10/$50 per million input/output tokens to $8/$40. Mythos 5.2 gets the same rates.

OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra still costs $10/$50 at its standard rates for prompts of up to 272,000 input tokens, putting Anthropic 20 percent below its rival on those token rates (at least for the time being).

Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens for either model, twice the standard rates.

Even after the price cut, Fable’s standard input and output rates are twice Opus 5.5’s current prices , though Anthropic’s new evaluations suggest that doesn’t necessarily translate into a higher cost per task.

Fable 5.2 targets complex coding

On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 scored 49.1 percent, compared with 32.4 percent for Fable 5.1, 45.5 percent for Opus 5.5, and 42.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra. On FrontierSWE v2, it scored 69.9 percent, ahead of Astra’s 65.5 percent and Opus’s 62.3 percent.

The cost comaprison with Opus may be even more interesting, though. In early FrontierCode 2.0 testing, Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort performed about as well as Opus 5.5 at Max effort for roughly half the cost per task.

Medium is now the default effort level for Fable 5.2 in Claude apps and Claude Code.

It’s worth noting that the results aren’t a clean sweep for Fable 5.2, though.

Gemini 4 Carbon leads Fable on AutomationBench, which tests business workflows, at 53.9 percent versus 51.4 percent. Meanwhile, Opus still retains a small lead on the Elo measure of AA-Briefcase v1.1, a knowledge-work evaluation.

Anthropic says Fable can act as an adviser that smaller models consult on harder problems, or as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to them. In one internal experiment, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder.

The company says it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced an OS that boots on a laptop, complete with drivers, persistent storage, a graphical interface, and an installer.

Fable promises fewer safety blocks

Anthropic says Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards remain as robust as those in 5.1. In early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, the company observed about 55 percent fewer blocks overall, including about 60 percent fewer in cybersecurity and 40 percent fewer in biology.

That could reduce interruptions to legitimate work, though fewer blocks don’t necessarily mean broader permissions. Fable still blocks high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing and exploit generation, as well as most research biology tasks. When a query is blocked, Anthropic says users instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity or Opus 5 for biology.

Direct Mythos access remains gated, but there is another route for enterprise security work: Claude Enterprise customers can use Claude Security, which now includes Mythos 5.2, even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program.

Anthropic also says it deliberately limited improvements in certain AI-development capabilities during training, including accelerator kernel optimization and work on large language model architectures. In those areas, the models perform at about Opus 5.5’s level, according to the company. It says those limits do not affect agentic coding, hardware development, or traditional machine learning research.

For API developers, Anthropic is expanding preserved thinking to all accounts. The feature restricts changes to Claude’s prior context that could be used to extract its reasoning for distillation.

Enterprise safeguards enter private beta

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , which the company first announced in September, is also moving into private beta, with Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe among the early customers. Automated safety monitoring runs on prompts and responses stored in customers’ own infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention, Anthropic says.

Eligible customers can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing the system. For other customers, Anthropic retains data for 30 days for safety monitoring.

Fable for physics

Anthropic argues that its models’ coding abilities also apply to scientific research because so much of that work is also based on software, including analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, or controlling instruments.

The company says Fable 5.2 solved two open theoretical-physics problems involving black holes and holographic duality. One involved completing a calculation proposed in 2003 to determine whether black-hole formation remains an abrupt transition in a small-universe quantum description. The other established the limit of a technique used to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe.

The Fermat claim is more specific than the early announcement suggested. Anthropic says a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean in 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Formalization expresses a proof in a language that a computer can check step by step; it is distinct from discovering a new proof.

The agents received a list of intermediate theorem statements to measure progress, but no mathematical references, according to Anthropic. An earlier research version of Claude took 11 days with a purpose-built harness and human guidance. The company’s comparison used a single run per model, with Opus 5.5 reaching 26 percent after 18 hours and making little additional progress by 30 hours.

Anthropic also tested Fable 5.2 on hardware design, working with circuit-board company Diode to produce a voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The company says Claude selected components, designed the boards and enclosures, and wrote the software. Diode built the boards, and its engineers tested and assembled the devices with Claude’s guidance.

All three worked without electrical modifications, according to Anthropic.

item.title: Google claims its new AI software cuts inference latency by over 90% — but there’s a catch
item.description:
Google’s eighth-generation TPU announcement on Monday included more than new chips, introducing TPU Sync , an open-source system designed to speed up AI inference by tackling a problem that worsens as context windows grow: moving data between different types of memory.

The software is made for developers running large models, particularly ones handling million-token contexts and reinforcement-learning workloads. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests.

The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests.

Inside the memory hierarchy

Written in C++, the framework moves data between accelerator memory, host DRAM, storage, and the network. It uses zero-copy transfers and native PjRtBuffer hardware descriptors to avoid unnecessary copies.

Combined host-to-device and device-to-host throughput reached 223 GB/s per Ironwood TPU host, approaching the theoretical 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 limit.

Google’s numbers, with caveats

In Google’s benchmarks , moving KV caches for the 235-billion-parameter Qwen3 model went from taking several seconds to about 230 milliseconds. That cut the average time to first token (TTFT) by 60% when relatively few requests were running at once. With a larger 480-billion-parameter model, the reduction reached 90%.

Google saw similar gains when testing prefix caching with 64,000-token contexts. TTFT dropped by as much as 90%, throughput increased by more than 50%, and P99 inter-token latency fell 30%. Developers may see different results depending on what they’re running, how much cached data they can reuse, and how much network bandwidth they have available.

SemiAnalysis , offers some context for the gains. Its analysis suggests that external TPU serving previously lacked the infrastructure needed to separate prefill and decode workloads effectively.

Where Nvidia still leads

Nvidia may still have an advantage in some workloads. SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX data shows its GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems ahead in parts of the disaggregated-serving performance curve, although a direct comparison with a fully tuned TPU v7 setup has yet to be published.

Chipping away at the CUDA moat

Developers can use the new software with the inference tools they already have since the company released the project alongside TorchTPU , with support for vLLM and SGLang , two widely used open-source inference engines. Developers already using those frameworks can run disaggregated workloads on TPUs without rebuilding their serving stack from scratch.

Developers already using those frameworks can run disaggregated workloads on TPUs without rebuilding their serving stack from scratch.

This also fits with Google’s broader effort to make its custom chips more competitive. The company has emphasized reducing inference costs through hardware changes, including reportedly designing chips around Gemini’s architecture .

Now it’s addressing the software problems that can leave those chips waiting for data. Making TPU infrastructure easier to use with familiar frameworks could give developers another reason to consider Google’s hardware instead of defaulting to Nvidia and CUDA; whether it can match Nvidia’s inference performance remains an open question.

Not production-ready yet

The software isn’t production-ready for everyone just yet. Google warns in its GitHub repository that the APIs are still changing and recommends sticking to a verified commit or tagged release. Support is also limited to Cloud TPU v7x and v6e, with specific JAX and PyTorch version requirements.

item.title: Cursor and Google join OpenAI in giving coding agents a voice. Claude Code stays silent.
item.description:
Two of the biggest players in the AI coding space are betting that developers want to talk to their agents while they work, with both announcing a two-way voice feature that lets users ask questions and give follow-up instructions without returning to the keyboard.

On Friday , Cursor announced Voice Chat with Agents , a Grok Voice -powered feature that lets developers call an agent and talk through a change. On the very same day, Google announced Voice mode in Antigravity , which uses Gemini Live to bring spoken conversations to its desktop app and command-line tool.

In a blog post announcing the feature, Nick Van der Auwermeulen , developer relations engineer at Google, contrasts the back-and-forth dynamic of human colleagues with the “rhythm” of working with coding agents.

“Some of the best engineering happens out loud,” Van der Auwermeulen writes. “You talk a bug through with a teammate, think out loud in front of a whiteboard, or say ‘ wait, try it the other way ’ halfway through a pairing session. Working with an agent has mostly had a different rhythm: you type a prompt, the agent works, you read what it did, and you type again.”

“Some of the best engineering happens out loud.”

The longer a job runs, he adds, the more often developers need to check in. A command might be waiting for approval, or a developer might spot a requirement the original instructions missed.

“Each of those moments pulls you back to the keyboard and away from whatever you were looking at,” he continues.

And so Antigravity’s voice mode keeps a live call open while the coding agent works, so the developer can hear an update or approve a command without reaching for the keyboard.

Cursor, for its part, makes a similar pitch for keeping the conversation going.

“Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward,” the company writes.

“Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward.”

Look who’s talking

Antigravity , for the uninitiated, is Google’s agentic software development platform. It debuted alongside Gemini 3 last November , with version 2.0 landing in May replete with a separate desktop app. There’s also a terminal client, Antigravity CLI , and extensions for developers who want to work from editors such as VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and Xcode.

Antigravity is now where Google is consolidating its various coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity in June, while it’s also in the midst of sunsetting Jules , a previously launched background coding agent.

It’s worth noting that Antigravity’s existing dictation feature already turns speech into a written prompt. Now, to start a two-way call in the desktop app, the user clicks the waveform button beside it and tells the agent what they want it to do.

Antigravity replies aloud and keeps the call open while the coding agent works, with the user able to ask how it’s going or give it further instructions. You can also interrupt the agent mid-sentence to ask a question or give it another instruction.

When the agent finishes, its written summary and a button to review the code changes appear in the same chat.

Additionally, voice mode also works in the Antigravity CLI. Users run the /voice live command to start a call, and hear the agent reply while it works away in the terminal.

Coding agents talk back

Cursor, which was acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in August for $60 billion, has followed a similar path toward embracing voice. It added dictation in October 2025 , and in release notes last month, the company said it had updated existing voice calls to let agents give short spoken progress updates.

One difference with Cursor’s rollout is where you can call from. Cursor supports voice chat on the web and iOS as well as on desktop, while Google offers it in the Antigravity desktop app and CLI. Cursor’s calls run on Grok Voice , which xAI launched through its API back in April .

“The push now, it seems, is to keep the conversation going after the agent starts work.”

However, Google and Cursor aren’t the first AI companies to bring two-way voice to coding agents. OpenAI launched a Codex desktop app in February with a built-in dictation feature . And as The New Stack reported in July , the company added two-way voice to Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app, letting developers give instructions and check on tasks by speaking. The Codex CLI has offered live voice conversations since the spring , with OpenAI enabling them by default in September .

Anthropic, for what it’s worth, has a voice mode which offers two-way voice functionality inside the Claude app only. In Claude Code, specifically, voice still only goes one way via dictation — the /voice command turns developers’ vocal instructions into prompt text , and the agent replies in writing.

Dictation itself is useful for describing a bug or sketching out a feature aloud, and it’s showing up across the AI coding landscape, from the major AI labs to well-funded startups such as Replit .

The push now, it seems, is to keep the conversation going after the agent starts work, so developers can follow up about a decision, clarify a requirement, or change direction before the work is finished.

item.title: Meta launches Muse Ember to take on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna
item.description:
Meta on Monday debuted Muse Ember, a smaller, more efficient multimodal member of its Muse model family.

The company is clearly taking a similar approach to the other frontier labs, with a family of models that cover everything from focused, high-volume tasks (think OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 ) to frontier intelligence like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, and, most recently, Meta’s Muse Wonder Full . And just like its competitors, Meta is pitching the smaller model for agentic subtasks like reading files, running tests, and making targeted fixes, with a larger model like Muse Wonder doing the planning.

Muse Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API under the model ID muse-ember-1.0 . It will likely soon be available on services like OpenRouter and on the neoclouds, too, given that Meta has done the same for its other Muse models in the past.

Like with previous Muse model releases, Meta is keeping Ember’s model weights private.

Ember is Meta’s take on a small, price-efficient model, and at least when it comes to the benchmarks, it’s a strong entry.

At max reasoning, Meta puts Ember at about $0.14 per task on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , compared with $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. Ember matches Haiku’s rounded score at about a third of the cost and scores higher than Luna for about a cent less per task.

At xhigh, the other Ember setting shown in Meta’s chart, the model scores about 34 at roughly $0.12 per task.

Muse Ember pricing

Ember, which has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 512K output tokens, is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Those input and output rates match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at their standard short-context prices. Both charge $0.01 per million cached input tokens at those rates, with higher prices for longer prompts. Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0 , with support for the Responses API.

How Chinese rivals compare

And while Meta doesn’t directly compare the new model to Chinese competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 , Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 Flash, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash in the chart, Ember undercuts the listed uncached input rates for all three. It also undercuts DeepSeek’s direct off-peak and MiniMax’s listed output prices and matches GLM’s. DeepSeek has a slightly lower off-peak cache-hit rate of $0.003 per million tokens.

On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, for example, Ember scores 36 at max reasoning, while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is at 33, MiniMax at 29, and GLM at 28. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, meanwhile, scores 28 on this same benchmark, while Haiku gets to 36, both at max reasoning.

Muse Ember vs. Muse Spark

Meta’s own Muse Spark 1.3 scores 37 at max reasoning and costs $2.39 per task at the standard API rates used in the comparison. Meta also offers a Spark Contributor tier, where it uses requests to improve its products. That tier matches Ember’s uncached input price and charges $0.20 per million output tokens.

Meta reports a lead over Haiku and Luna on its own Personal Superintelligence Index, a measure of personal and knowledge work. One benchmark where Ember doesn’t fare as well is FrontierCode 2.0, which evaluates whether a repository maintainer would merge an agent’s changes. Ember scores 27.2 percent, compared with 34.9 percent for Haiku and 28.5 percent for DeepSeek. Spark 1.3 scores 23.1 percent.

Computer use on OSWorld

Ember can take text, images, audio, and video as inputs, and Meta says it can operate desktop apps from screenshots.

On OSWorld 2.1 , it got nearly the same partial-credit score as Haiku, 69.5 percent versus 68.9 percent, but finished more tasks outright, 33.8 percent versus 27.8 percent for Haiku and 17 percent for Luna. In a separate OSWorld 2.1 run, Spark 1.3 earned nearly identical partial credit to Ember and completed 39.25 percent of tasks.

Meta says the new model is the first it trained using the larger Muse Wonder Full model. That’s similar to what the company did with Muse Wonder to train the specialized models it began rolling out to its Muse personal agent and Meta AI .

item.title: Why semantic layers will be essential for enterprise AI
item.description:
AI can find your data. It can’t read your mind. AI agents can already reach into your CRM, your warehouse, and your ERP, and with standards like MCP , that list keeps growing. Access is solved. Understanding is not. An agent can retrieve every record in your pipeline and still give your CRO the wrong answer, not because the data is bad, but because it doesn’t know what you mean by “pipeline.” Agents without semantics don’t fail loudly. They deliver confident answers to the wrong question.

“Pipeline” means something different at every company

Ask an executive, “How is pipeline looking this quarter?” and it sounds like a simple request. It isn’t. The answer depends on your sales stages, your forecasting methodology, your territory structure, and your qualification criteria, which are business rules that evolved over years, often without ever being written down. Two companies can use the same word and mean entirely different things. Businesses don’t run on raw data. They run on shared meaning, and humans carry that meaning around in their heads. Agents don’t have heads. They have whatever we give them.

From systems of record to systems of agency

That matters more as the way we work changes. For decades, employees logged into the CRM, the BI tool, or the ERP and supplied the judgment themselves, because they knew which dashboard to trust and which field was never quite right. Now they state intent, and an agent figures out the rest.

The systems of record stay where they are, but a new layer sits between people and technology: a system of agency. In my experience, leaders spend a lot of time asking whether that layer can connect to everything and far less time asking whether it understands anything. If that layer doesn’t understand your business, nothing underneath it matters.

Catalogs helped people find data. Semantic layers help AI understand it.

For the last decade, we invested in governance, integration, quality, and catalogs, and those investments still matter because trusted data is the prerequisite. But a catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means. It captures what your best people carry in their heads:

  • Business definitions, such as what counts as “pipeline,” “churn,” or “active customer”
  • Policies that govern how data can be used
  • Relationships between products, customers, contracts, and outcomes
  • Rules that determine how decisions get made

“A catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means.”

Put that in a form both humans and machines can consume, and agents stop guessing. This isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s the difference between an agent that is technically capable and one that is operationally reliable.

Relationships are where the value lives

Definitions are only half the story, because business decisions rarely live in a single dataset. They depend on how concepts connect. Take an AI-powered quoting process, where the agent needs products, contracts, customer history, usage patterns, approval structures, and pricing rules all at once, and each lives in a different system. Retrieving them is the easy part.

Reasoning across them is the hard part, and when the agent gets it wrong, it won’t throw an error. It will produce a plausible quote with the wrong discount and send it to a real customer. That’s where knowledge graphs and context graphs earn their place. They treat information as connected business knowledge rather than isolated facts, so instead of piecing together a customer’s story from scattered records, the agent gets a map of how your business fits together.

Meaning is also an efficiency play

Without encoded context, agents spend compute rediscovering relationships and re-inferring meaning your organization already understands, so every query becomes a small act of reconstruction. Define it once, and every agent reasons from the same source. That means more consistent answers, fewer contradictions between teams, and lower cost as usage scales. Consistency is underrated. If sales, finance, and operations each get a different answer to the same question from the same AI, you haven’t built intelligence. You’ve built an argument.

Anyone can build now. Not everything should scale.

Generative AI has finally delivered on the citizen developer promise. Employees can describe a workflow in plain language and get a working prototype back, which means good ideas can now come from anywhere. That’s the opportunity.

“If sales, finance, and operations each get a different answer to the same question from the same AI, you haven’t built intelligence. You’ve built an argument.”

The risk is that a tool that helps one person is a convenience, while the same tool deployed across departments is a liability if no one validated it, governed it, or owns it. Organizations need a path from experiment to enterprise asset. I think of it as a graduation factory: identify the promising prototypes, test them, apply governance, and promote the ones that earn it. Innovation should be easy to start and hard to scale carelessly.

The same foundations apply here. Only 12% of organizations say their data is AI-ready , and only 31% can tie their AI initiatives to clear KPIs. Semantics and governance are how you close that gap.

Where I’d start

You don’t need a multi-year program to make progress. Start small and prove it:

  1. Pick the five terms your executives argue about most, and define them.
  2. Assign a business owner to each definition.
  3. Expose those definitions to your agents through a governed layer, then measure whether the answers improve.

Meaning, like data, has to be managed. Someone has to own it.

The bottom line

Connecting AI to your data is table stakes. Everyone will do it, so it won’t differentiate you. Trusted data is the prerequisite. Shared meaning is the multiplier. Connect your agents to everything, and you’ve built access. Teach them how your business thinks, and you’ve built an advantage.

item.title: Real-time state has a cost your memory bill won’t show
item.description:
Real-time applications often combine tools with distinct roles. A typical setup might use Kafka to handle events, Flink to process them, Redis to serve the latest state, and a database to maintain the system of record. Applications that use vector search may add a vector store, too.

This division of responsibilities offers flexibility and independent scaling. It also creates costs when data moves between components or when overlapping state is maintained in more than one place.

“The copies to question are those maintained largely because processing happens in one system and applications read the results from another.”

Some of those copies are necessary. Replicas protect against failures, checkpoints help systems recover, and durable event logs preserve history. They’re worth paying for. The copies to question are those maintained largely because processing happens in one system and applications read the results from another.

Take a velocity counter tracking a payment card’s transactions over the past five minutes. Flink calculates the count and maintains keyed state to support that computation.

But a fraud-scoring service also needs to retrieve the result. Flink’s internal state isn’t designed for general-purpose serving, and Flink deprecated its Queryable State feature in 1.18. A common solution is to publish the count to Redis.

That gives applications a dedicated serving layer, with its own scaling and operational requirements. Flink’s working state and the Redis value may overlap but not be identical, and each published update involves serialization, network traffic, and processing before consumers see it.

Where consistency gets complicated

Keeping state synchronized gets more complicated when applications span availability zones.

Consider a hypothetical payment system that serves reads from asynchronous replicas in several availability zones to reduce cross-zone traffic. A refund goes through, but the update is still making its way to one of those replicas.

A service reading from it could see the transaction as not yet refunded and issue another refund, even though the first has already been processed. Without coordination between the refund paths, the customer could be paid twice.

“Without coordination between the refund paths, the customer could be paid twice.”

This is an application-design concern wherever decisions depend on asynchronously replicated state. Putting processing and storage on the same platform wouldn’t necessarily prevent it.

The immediate issue is replica lag, combined with an application that decides without atomically checking and updating the state that authorizes the refund. If the refund calls an external payment service, that service also needs an idempotent request mechanism so retries cannot issue the same refund twice.

A separate processing-and-serving design also introduces a publication delay: the processor may calculate an updated value before the serving store receives it. That’s export lag, distinct from replica lag within the serving store. During that lag, a burst of fraudulent transactions can be scored against an out-of-date count. Export lag and replica lag can leave applications reading stale data, but neither should be confused with the check-then-act race that could cause the duplicate refund.

Hazelcast can avoid the separate publication step for workloads where computation runs directly against stored state. Its entry processors can atomically update individual map entries on the member holding the relevant key. That doesn’t make the system automatically strongly consistent during network partitions, though.

Applications needing stronger coordination can use appropriately configured data structures in Hazelcast’s Raft-based CP subsystem . Using it does not turn an ordinary IMap into a strongly consistent map, or make a map update atomic with an external payment. Separate processing and storage systems can also use strongly consistent coordination.

The cost of moving state

Memory tends to dominate discussions of in-memory architectures, but CPU and networking costs can matter just as much.

A 2025 paper from UC Berkeley and Databricks, Rethinking the Cost of Distributed Caches for Datacenter Services , examined caching economics using synthetic workloads, Meta traces, and production data from Databricks’ Unity Catalog.

“Memory tends to dominate discussions of in-memory architectures, but CPU and networking costs can matter just as much.”

Using the paper’s Google Cloud pricing assumptions of roughly $17 per vCPU-month and $2 per gigabyte-month of memory, the researchers found that adding in-memory caching cut operating costs by a factor of three to four. The CPU savings outweighed the cost of the additional RAM.

That isn’t a comparison of Hazelcast against Flink and Redis; the study compares caching with no caching. Its remote-versus-linked-cache comparison supports the narrower argument that communication and serialization consume CPU.

The paper also found that per-read version checks for stronger consistency could erase much of the cost benefit, so comparisons need equivalent consistency requirements.

A 2019 paper by Google researchers, “Fast Key-Value Stores: An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone,” reported a 40% reduction in p99.9 latency for ProtoCache, a component of a Google application, after moving from a remote key-value store to an architecture that keeps application logic and in-memory state together .

A separate, illustrative calculation shows the memory cost of maintaining two equivalent working sets. At the paper’s assumed memory price, 400 GB would represent about $800 a month in memory alone, before backups, checkpoints, and other infrastructure.

Maintaining an equivalent amount in both processing and serving tiers would double that figure, although Flink’s intermediate state and the results published to Redis can differ substantially.

Then there’s the work involved in keeping the systems synchronized. Each update must be serialized, transmitted, and processed, and both platforms require monitoring, scaling, and maintenance.

One way to get a sense of this overhead is to count the steps involved in a single read-modify-write operation. With separate processing and serving systems, an event might be ingested, keyed state updated, the result serialized and published, then written to the serving store before an application reads it. That’s potentially four or five serialization or network steps for one update. Running the computation where the state is stored can reduce that to a single step. It’s not a precise measure of cost, but tracing the path of an update can help identify where CPU time and network resources are being spent.

A fair total-cost comparison also needs node counts, instance types, licensing, discounts, and equivalent managed-versus-self-managed deployments. The $800 figure is memory arithmetic, not a total-cost estimate or measured Hazelcast saving.

Bringing computation closer to the data

Hazelcast provides one way to bring processing closer to stored data . Rather than sending information back and forth between separate systems, it distributes data across cluster members according to key and can run computations on the member that holds it. It keeps backup copies in case a member fails.

Hazelcast offers two approaches, depending on the kind of processing involved. Hazelcast’s Jet engine can maintain internal state for windowed stream calculations and publish results to a distributed map that applications can read.

That intermediate state and the result-publication step still exist on the same platform; processing, map writes, and backups may also involve traffic between members. Kafka can remain the durable event log in either design, and the database of record can remain in place.

For applications that need to update stored values directly, Hazelcast also has entry processors . These run code against the map entry itself, rather than calculating a result elsewhere and then copying it across.

Take the transaction counter discussed earlier. An entry processor could maintain per-minute transaction counts in a distributed map, and the application could sum the most recent five buckets to calculate the total. This avoids the need for a timer to remove expired transactions, though the result would be accurate to the minute rather than the second. The application would still need to account for late or duplicate events.

Keep entry processors lightweight, since a long-running operation can block other work on the same partition. Network traffic still occurs between clients and the cluster, and Hazelcast still maintains backup copies.

Serialization costs also depend on the map’s in-memory format : the default BINARY format stores serialized values, while OBJECT can reduce conversion work for entry processing. The difference is that, for workloads suited to this approach, there’s no separate processing tier that needs to keep publishing updates to the serving store.

When separate systems make sense

Keeping processing and storage apart has one significant advantage: each can scale independently.

Consider an application running complex decision rules that produce little more than a yes-or-no answer. It might need substantial CPU capacity but very little storage. A separate processing tier allows teams to add compute resources without expanding the serving infrastructure.

Other applications hold large amounts of state but do relatively little processing. Putting both workloads on one cluster may offer limited savings, particularly if CPU-intensive tasks compete with latency-sensitive reads.

Separate platforms also allow independent deployments, workload isolation, and access to specialized processing features. Hazelcast can offer some of that flexibility within a single cluster, too. Its lite members handle compute tasks without storing data, allowing teams to dedicate regular members to storage and add compute capacity separately.

For some workloads, keeping processing and storage on entirely separate platforms will still make sense. But when applications frequently read and update the same state, Hazelcast can reduce data movement between systems.

What to measure before making the switch

The starting point should be a profile of the existing deployment. How much CPU time goes into application logic, and how much is spent serializing data or communicating across the network? How much state is actually duplicated between processing and serving?

Average response times won’t tell the whole story, either. A system might perform well most of the time but slow down considerably on certain requests. That’s why it’s worth checking p99 and p99.9 request latency, along with throughput and end-to-end latency: the time from an event arriving to its result being readable, including any export lag.

Run the comparison with the same workload, the same end-to-end latency target, and the same durability guarantees. Failure testing matters as well: check recovery time, replay behavior, duplicate handling, and correctness during node failures and network partitions. Backup copies and recovery mechanisms add to the infrastructure bill.

For some applications, independently scaling processing and storage will remain the better choice. Others may find they’re paying to move data between systems when they could do the same work directly against application-accessible state.

Not every copy is unnecessary. Replicas protect against failures, checkpoints support recovery, and stream processors need intermediate state. The copies worth questioning are those maintained largely because processing and serving happen in different systems.

item.title: Moving from AI adoption to an AI operating model: How Docusign engineering went beyond tool rollout
item.description:
Docusign rolled out AI coding tools across its engineering teams, expecting them to help developers write code faster and do more. Initial enthusiasm was high, but early gains plateaued.

By June 2025, Docusign had reached a sticking point. According to its engineering team’s account , 49% of engineers were actively using AI coding tools, while a reported 18% improvement in developer productivity had leveled off. Engineers still needed time to experiment, guidance tailored to Docusign’s codebase, and help fitting the tools into their day-to-day work.

Docusign now reports that all of its more than 1,100 engineers are onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools

CTO Sagnik Nandy believes getting people to use the technology is only the beginning.

“There’s a big difference between trying to get a few wins versus doing it consistently and doing it right,” Nandy tells The New Stack .

Docusign responded by changing how it introduced and measured AI across engineering, moving beyond coding assistants toward reusable agents and automated workflows.

Why Docusign turned to its engineers

Instead of making AI adoption mandatory, Docusign established a six-person Eng AI Champions team to develop guardrails, share engineering practices, and run workshops. Docusign reports that adoption reached 65% by October 2025. The company then extended that work through AI Multipliers embedded in individual development teams. Nandy says around 75 Multipliers helped teammates put the shared practices into use and fed problems back to the central team.

Docusign for Developers is a powerful suite of tools and resources designed to help developers build the solutions, workflows, and integrations their organizations and customers need across the entire agreement lifecycle.
Learn More

“They were tasked with two things,” Nandy explains. “The decisions, the solutions we built, they had to deploy it within their team, and also get feedback in terms of what’s working, what’s not working, and what’s missing.”

Docusign’s account of the initiative showed that active usage reached 93% within two months of introducing the Multipliers, while lines of code updated per developer increased by approximately 52% from the company’s starting point. That code-volume measure does not, by itself, establish a matching improvement in delivery speed or software quality.

Nandy believes the combination of central coordination and feedback from individual teams has helped sustain the program, an approach he has also discussed in an engineering leadership podcast .

“When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out.”

“When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out,” he says. “I think the reason that hasn’t happened for us … is because we already have such a rich body of information and feedback flowing in, and people acting on it and then redeploying things.”

Teaching AI to ‘speak Docusign’

Once engineers were comfortable using AI for coding, Docusign began looking at entire development workflows. That required tools with access to its repositories, architecture, telemetry, and internal practices, so assistants could work with the company’s own context.

“Our solutions and agents, we joke, they speak Docusign,” Nandy says. “They know which internal tools to go look into, what our internal coding guardrails are, guidelines are, what system choices we make, where information resides for disambiguating between different pieces of information.”

Nandy describes several internal tools for different engineering tasks: Kody for Docusign-specific coding work, Chronicle for observability and incident investigation, and DocuWiki for code-aware internal documentation. Docusign’s engineering blog also describes an AI-assisted code review tool for identifying potential architectural and security issues during review.

Krew brings these capabilities together , allowing teams to build agents called Krewmates for recurring tasks and more complex workflows.

“One of the things that the Eng AI Champions and Multipliers did is they identified end-to-end flows, and we wanted to improve the entire flow,” Nandy says.

He describes an internal agent that runs overnight, searches error logs for problems, and prepares proposed fixes.

“Come morning, the engineer is greeted with, ‘Hey, here’s a PR. This was an issue we found, and this is the fix.’ It’s magical.”

In Nandy’s example, Krew coordinates the workflow, drawing on telemetry from Chronicle and Kody’s coding capabilities. The engineer then reviews the proposed pull request.

Docusign gives another example . For a task involving infrastructure configuration files, the agent correctly modified 10 of 12 files on its first pass in about 15 minutes, using a sample commit as guidance. The company says the process previously took roughly a week of engineer time. The first pass still left two files to correct; it was not a finished, approved change in 15 minutes.

Making successful workflows reusable

An agent built for one team has limited value if everyone else has to recreate it.

Docusign’s Krew orchestration platform allows engineers to discover, copy, and extend Krewmates connected to internal systems. These agents can handle recurring tasks, respond to triggers, and involve people when needed.

“We’ve taken a very open approach,” Nandy says. “All the Krewmates are visible to everyone. You can see how much they are getting used. It’s extremely easy to copy and extend them.”

Frequently used Krewmates become more visible, helping teams find existing solutions rather than building their own from scratch.

“If something is good, you can try to teach 1,000 other people to do it, or you can make it easy for 1,000 other people to inherit it.”

“If something is good, you can try to teach 1,000 other people to do it, or you can make it easy for 1,000 other people to inherit it. And we went for the latter.”

The approach also depends on maintaining those shared tools, documenting changes, and feeding problems back to the teams responsible for improving them. Docusign’s Krew team reports that apparently successful runs sometimes left duplicate posts or partial outputs, prompting improvements to run tracking and observability. For leaders adopting this model, a durable workflow needs a named owner, a way to report failures, and periodic checks on quality and running costs.

Measuring what matters

Docusign’s adoption figures show how widely AI has spread, but Nandy is wary of treating usage as the ultimate measure of success.

“We’ve been very focused on value as opposed to anecdotes or gimmicks,” he says. “The way to do that is you keep moving up the value chain.”

Initially, Docusign measured how many engineers were using AI, followed by how much code they were generating. Nandy says the next questions concern whether teams are actually delivering better results.

“Adoption, so what? … Are you doing more?” he says. “Then you look at feature velocity. Are you shipping things sooner?”

Docusign also considers customer satisfaction and reliability, particularly whether faster development introduces problems elsewhere.

For engineering leaders, that means examining delivery times, review latency, testing, rework, and incident investigation rather than relying solely on adoption percentages or lines of AI-generated code.

Guardrails before speed

Giving agents more responsibility doesn’t mean removing human accountability.

“Any PR, it’s the responsibility of the individual signing off on it,” Nandy says. “No code goes unreviewed into the system.”

Docusign says its autonomous coding agent runs tests before submitting pull requests, with human review, AI-generated-code labels, and quality gates required before merging. Its AI Innovation Principles emphasize human oversight and safeguards. Krew’s documentation makes the boundary explicit: an agent cannot merge a pull request or take an irreversible action without a person’s approval.

Nandy compares AI to a chainsaw: a powerful tool that can accomplish more than traditional alternatives, but requires appropriate safeguards.

“You need very different gear when you have a chainsaw, otherwise you can hurt yourself.”

“You need very different gear when you have a chainsaw, otherwise you can hurt yourself,” he says. “It’s important to get that right.”

He also warns against introducing AI where conventional software would work better. Some of Docusign’s internal solutions were developed using AI but run as deterministic processes without continually invoking a model.

“I often see people throwing AI at problems that probably don’t need AI,” Nandy says.

Beyond the rollout

For Nandy, Docusign’s approach rests on five principles: measure value, make successful solutions reusable, keep costs and governance sustainable, establish guardrails and build in the organization’s own context.

Together, these principles support a shift from encouraging engineers to try AI to workflows that teams can maintain, measure, and improve across teams. The practical next step for an engineering leader is to choose a well-defined workflow, agree on the outcome to measure, assign an owner, and specify where human approval is required before expanding it.

The lesson for engineering leaders is that adoption alone won’t deliver lasting results. Teams also need shared tools, clear ownership, engineer feedback, and measures that show whether the work is actually getting better.

More details are available on Docusign’s Engineering blog , alongside its current engineering opportunities .

item.title: Scaling an autonomous agent from one team to fifty: A serverless-to-container decision framework
item.description:
QA teams shipping complex products generate test failures around the clock. Every failure needs a bug ticket with steps, screenshots, repro rates, and regression labels. The manual process takes 10-15 minutes per failure. Multiply that by 30+ failures per week across a team, and you have burned an entire engineering day on documentation that should be automatic.

I built a system to eliminate this entirely. Not a dashboard. Not a notification bot. An autonomous agent that observes test results, makes judgment calls – is this a new bug, a duplicate, or a regression? And takes action without human intervention. It files structured bugs, attaches screenshots, calculates repro rates, detects regressions build-over-build, and notifies the right people. The team just marks FAIL and moves on.

The system runs on Lambda today. It works perfectly for one team. But what happens when other teams want it? What happens when you need to serve 10, 50, or 100 teams? That’s where the architectural decisions get interesting – not because Lambda fails, but because the workload characteristics shift into territory where a different tool becomes the better fit.

What I built (and why it works)

The architecture is elegant: an EventBridge rule triggers a Lambda function every 15 minutes. The function polls the test management API, processes failures through a decision engine (dedup check against DynamoDB, regression detection against previous build results), and files bugs via the JIRA API. Total infrastructure cost: under $5/month.

AWS Marketplace helps companies of all sizes find, try, buy, deploy, and manage solutions from AWS Partners. Accelerate solution discovery, improve governance, enhance cost transparency, and reduce SaaS sprawl with centralized billing and management on AWS.
Learn More
Hear more from our sponsor

Lambda was the correct choice here for three reasons:

  1. Zero operational overhead: No servers, no scaling config, no patching. Deploy and forget.
  2. Cost proportional to usage: One team generates ~200 invocations/month. At Lambda pricing, this is effectively free.
  3. Fast iteration: The decision engine went through 20+ revisions in the first month. Lambda’s deployment model let me ship changes in seconds.

Within weeks of deploying, the system filed more complete and consistent bugs than the team had ever produced manually. Zero missed failures. Regressions caught in minutes instead of days. Status interruptions to QA dropped to zero because anyone could query the system directly via Slack. 8-10 hours per week saved.

Other teams have noticed. “Can we have that?” is a recurring question. The answer seems simple – deploy another instance per team. But at scale, the workload characteristics change in ways that shift the architectural decision.

The scaling decision

Lambda handles single-tenant agentic workloads beautifully. The challenge at multi-tenant scale isn’t that Lambda can’t do it; it’s that the workload characteristics shift:

From stateless events to long-running context: A single team’s poll cycle finishes in seconds. But cross-project correlation – “is this the same failure pattern we’re seeing across three teams?” requires analyzing hundreds of results and their relationships in a single pass. That’s a fundamentally different compute profile.

From isolated invocations to shared resource contention: When 50 functions trigger on the same EventBridge schedule, they all hit TestRail and JIRA APIs simultaneously. You need centralized rate limiting, connection pooling, and backpressure – patterns that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure.

From single-team to multi-tenant isolation: Each team needs guaranteed resources, network boundaries, and scoped credentials. The isolation model becomes as important as the compute model.

Lambda’s recent launches address many of these individually – Managed Instances solve connection persistence, Durable Functions break the 15-minute ceiling for long-running workflows, and Tenant Isolation provides native tenant boundaries. For many multi-tenant workloads, these capabilities narrow the gap significantly.

But for this specific workload – long-running agents that need persistent connections, cross-tenant analysis, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation simultaneously- the decision framework points toward a container-native execution model with serverless-like operations. That’s where EKS Auto Mode fits.

The decision framework

This led me to build a simple decision rubric – not Lambda vs. containers, but which characteristics does your workload actually exhibit?

“The deciding factor for my workload: I need all of the right-column characteristics simultaneously. Together, they compose more naturally in a container-native environment.”

The deciding factor for my workload: I need all of the right-column characteristics simultaneously. Cross-team pattern detection requires a shared analysis context. ML-based bug classification requires burst GPU. Per-team isolation requires namespace-level boundaries. Centralized rate limiting requires a persistent shared service. Each of these is individually solvable in Lambda. Together, they compose more naturally in a container-native environment.

What unlocks at scale: cross-team intelligence

The most interesting architectural capability that emerges at multi-tenant scale isn’t per-team automation – it’s cross-team pattern detection. This is what makes the scaling exercise worthwhile.

Cross-team failure correlation

When 50 teams run their test suites independently, failures appear isolated. But patterns emerge across teams that no single team can see:

  • Three teams report navigation failures on the same firmware build → systemic regression, not three independent bugs
  • Test failures correlate with deployment timing across unrelated services → infrastructure issue, not product bugs
  • Identical error signatures across teams with different test suites → shared dependency failure

This requires an analysis engine that can hold context from all teams simultaneously – comparing fingerprints, correlating timestamps, and identifying shared root causes. That’s a persistent, long-running workload with access to cross-tenant state. It runs naturally as a shared service in a platform namespace, consuming events from all tenant agents.

ML-based bug classification

Once you have enough historical data (thousands of bugs filed across teams), patterns become classifiable:

  • Auto-assign bugs to the correct component owner based on failure signature
  • Predict severity based on failure characteristics (crash vs. degraded behavior vs. cosmetic)
  • Suggest related bugs for investigation (“this looks like the same root cause as PROJ-4521”)
  • Detect anomalous failure rates before they become incident-scale

This inference workload is bursty – you need GPU when bugs arrive, not 24/7. A GPU NodePool that scales to zero when idle and provisions g5 instances only during inference keeps costs proportional to actual usage. The same pod that files a bug can synchronously call the classification service, get a component assignment, and include it in the ticket – all within the same request path.

Queryable knowledge base via Slack

The agent isn’t just an automation – it becomes the organization’s queryable QA state. Via Slack, anyone can ask:

  • “What’s the failure rate for navigation this week across all teams?”
  • “Show me regressions introduced in build 2.4.1”
  • “Which teams are seeing the most P0 bugs right now?”

This transforms the agent from a task automator into an intelligence layer. The answers require cross-team state aggregation, trend computation, and natural language interpretation – all served from persistent, indexed state that accumulates over time.

What EKS Auto Mode brings to this architecture

EKS Auto Mode launched at re:Invent 2024 with a specific promise: full Kubernetes without managing nodes. For a multi-tenant agent platform, this means:

  • Nodes appear when pods need them. Deploy a tenant namespace with an auto-filer pod. The Karpenter-based scheduler provisions a node within seconds. When the pod is deleted (tenant offboarded), the node is consolidated or terminated automatically. You never think about EC2 instances.
  • Security is not your configuration burden. Nodes run immutable Bottlerocket AMIs – read-only root filesystem, SELinux enforcing, no SSH access. Nodes rotate every 21 days automatically. For long-running agent pods, this means a graceful drain roughly every three weeks. At most one missed poll cycle.
  • Scaling is reactive to demand. During off-hours when agents are idle between polls, Auto Mode consolidates workloads onto fewer nodes. You pay for what you use.
  • GPU workloads slot in without architectural changes. Define a GPU NodePool for the ML classification service. EKS Auto Mode provisions g5 instances only when inference pods are scheduled and terminates them when done.

The multi-tenant architecture

At scale, the system would have three layers:

  1. Shared platform services: a rate limiter that prevents any single tenant from exhausting external API quotas, a connection pool manager that maintains persistent sessions to TestRail and JIRA, and a Prometheus instance collecting metrics across all tenants.
  2. Per-tenant agent namespaces: each team gets an isolated namespace containing their auto-filer pod, reporter pod, and Slack bot pod. ResourceQuotas guarantee resources. NetworkPolicies enforce that Team A’s pods cannot talk to Team B’s pods. Each namespace’s service account assumes a tenant-scoped IAM role via IRSA.
  3. Shared ML inference namespace: GPU-enabled pods running classification models that all tenants can call. This namespace has its own NodePool that scales to zero when no inference is happening.

The agent code would remain essentially the same Python that runs on Lambda today – the core decision engine (observe, dedup, decide, act) doesn’t change. What changes is the execution model: instead of being invoked per-event and destroyed, the agent runs as a long-lived async loop with persistent connections, graceful shutdown handling, and internal scheduling.

The AWS portfolio working together

The right framing isn’t “migrate off Lambda onto EKS.” It’s “use each service where it fits”:

  • Lambda remains the entry point. New teams start here. Single-team automation at $5/month with zero ops. Event-driven triggers, rapid iteration, pay-per-invocation economics.
  • Lambda + Durable Functions handles teams that need longer analysis windows or multi-step orchestration without leaving the serverless model.
  • EKS Auto Mode serves the platform layer when you need persistent multi-tenant services, cross-team intelligence, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation working together.
  • DynamoDB persists state across all layers – dedup records, bug history, trend data.
  • EventBridge orchestrates events whether the consumer is a Lambda function or a Kubernetes pod.

A team that needs 30-minute analysis windows or multi-step workflows (poll → correlate → file → notify → wait for response → update) benefits from Durable Functions without leaving serverless. You stay here until you need cross-tenant shared state or GPU – that’s the signal to evaluate Auto Mode.

“Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.”

The intelligence moves up the stack as the organization’s needs mature. Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.

Key takeaways

  • Start serverless: Lambda lets you validate the agentic pattern at zero operational cost. The $5/month price point removes all friction for proving the concept works. Don’t prematurely optimize for scale you don’t have.
  • Design for portability from day one: Structure your Lambda function as a pure decision engine with external state. Containerizing it means wrapping it in an async loop and adding a health endpoint. If you build Lambda functions as self-contained decision engines rather than tightly coupled to the invocation model, the transition is a one-day exercise whenever you need it.
  • The decision trigger isn’t scale – it’s workload characteristics: Don’t move because you hit 50 teams. Move when you need capabilities that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure: cross-team correlation, centralized rate limiting, GPU inference, streaming connections.
  • Multi-tenancy is an isolation problem, not a compute problem: Both Lambda (Tenant Isolation) and Kubernetes (namespaces) solve this. Choose based on what other characteristics your workload needs alongside isolation.
  • EKS Auto Mode closes the operational gap: Before Auto Mode, choosing EKS meant accepting node management overhead. Auto Mode removes that tradeoff. You get container-native execution with serverless-like operations.

The cost math

Single team on Lambda today: $3-5/month. 8-10 hours/week saved. 67x ROI. Fifty teams on EKS Auto Mode would cost approximately $200-250/month total – roughly $4-5 per team per month. Same per-team economics as Lambda, but with namespace isolation, persistent connections, GPU-ready infrastructure, centralized observability, and built-in organizational governance.

The cost-per-team barely changes. What changes is what you get for it!

What comes next?

The agentic pattern – ‘observe, decide, act’ is infrastructure-agnostic. The decision logic doesn’t care about its deployment target. What changes is what becomes possible when agents stop operating in isolation.

“The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents.”

The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents. An auto-filer agent detects a failure pattern and hands context to a root-cause agent, which traces the dependency chain across services, identifies the offending commit, and drafts a fix recommendation – all before a human sees the bug ticket. Agent-to-agent delegation, where one agent’s output becomes another’s input without human routing in between.

Beyond that: agents that build their own decision models. Today, I hand-code the dedup logic and regression detection rules. Tomorrow, the agent observes which of its filed bugs humans close as duplicates, learns from those corrections, and tightens its own classification boundaries. The system improves not because I ship better code, but because it accumulates organizational judgment over time.

The system started as a weekend project to stop filing bugs manually. It now runs in production, eliminating an entire category of manual work from QA operations.

The infrastructure question stays the same – serverless for validation, containers for scale. But the agents running on that infrastructure are about to get significantly more capable. Teams with the platform layer ready will be the ones that can adopt those capabilities without rearchitecting.

item.title: Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab
item.description:
Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The challenge is keeping everything in sync, especially when agents are working at the same time, sharing project state, and operating with different permissions.

Announced Wednesday , Teammates builds on infrastructure Perplexity has spent much of the year developing. The launch puts that earlier work to use in workflows where agents can delegate tasks and continue operating across sessions.

The challenge of keeping agents stateful

When Nate Kupp , Perplexity’s vice president of infrastructure, took The New Stack inside the company’s agent sandboxes , he described the difficulty of maintaining reliable systems at that scale.

“Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build,” Kupp said, pointing to the durability and uptime requirements of operating millions of sandboxes.

“Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build”

Teammates relies on Perplexity Computer’s existing infrastructure, which separates persistent project state from individual execution environments. That allows agents to continue working on the same project without depending on a single uninterrupted session.

Shared state lives in Git

In a technical breakdown of its shared workspaces , the company described how it uses Git-backed repositories to keep project state intact across sessions. Each Computer project has its own repository, while agents work in separate sandboxes and submit their changes back to the shared project.

That gets more complicated when agents are working on the same code at once since if one agent commits its changes first, another may have to reapply its work against the latest version.

Perplexity says fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected because they’re based on outdated repository state. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds.

Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds.

Memory is handled separately through Perplexity’s Brain system, which keeps what agents have learned in dedicated repositories. That lets background agents update shared knowledge without interfering with changes to the project’s files.

Pausing and forking agents

Perplexity built SPACE around Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots, making it possible to pause, resume, or fork agent sessions without losing their saved state.

With Teammates, developers can connect tools like Slack and GitHub and set up triggers that tell agents when to act. Perplexity hasn’t said much about what happens when that work gets stuck, particularly when one agent is waiting on another or acting on information that’s already out of date.

The open permission questions

Each teammate runs in its own isolated environment and browser session, with access managed through Computer’s existing permissions and credentials handled securely through encryption. Users can also monitor progress and take control when needed.

It’s unclear how it prevents agents from accessing resources beyond their permissions when tasks are handed off. For enterprises, that uncertainty could influence how much autonomy they’re willing to give agents without requiring human approval.

Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned.
