Hear more from our sponsor

I stopped asking whether my agent was functioning and focused on a narrower diagnostic question: If I intentionally break the system, which metrics actually detect the failure?

Intentionally breaking the agent

The target system is a customer support agent interacting with a mock enterprise API spanning 30 scoped operations across tickets, users, billing, subscriptions, files, and messages. Every API call writes to an append-only audit log, and each task concludes with a state change that an external script verifies mechanically against the database. The suite contains 19 standard scored tasks alongside the two refund traps.

I established a baseline using Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) with full administrative privileges across three identical runs. Evaluating three baseline replicates is critical: a detection system that fires false positives on an unmodified setup is useless. Every detection threshold reflects the baseline variance doubled to account for real-world statistical distribution.

I then introduced eight specific regressions—one per test run—to simulate common production failure modes :

  • Weaker model: Executed the standard prompt using Claude Haiku 5.5.
  • Speed pressure: Added a single instruction directing the agent to minimize API calls and skip optional read operations.
  • Truncated documentation: Restricted the API documentation to list only 11 of the 30 available commands.
  • Missing scope: Revoked one required permission per task from the credential grant.
  • Stale reads: Routed read queries to an asynchronous replica that lagged behind primary writes.
  • Flaky upstream API: Intercepted a deterministic 25% of API calls with transient errors.
  • Slow upstream API: Introduced 1.5 seconds of artificial latency to every network call.
  • Distractor tool: Exposed a deprecated alias alongside the valid close-ticket command that accepted calls without mutating state.

Six of these eight regressions execute inside the API behind a per-run wrapper script, ensuring deterministic, reproducible failure paths.

Before evaluating detector sensitivity, I verified that each injection actively affected the execution environment. A detector cannot catch an idle regression. The logs confirmed the flaky API arm intercepted 31 calls, the stale read arm served 18 outdated queries, and the missing-scope arm triggered 19 authorization denials.

The distractor arm invoked the deprecated alias zero times because the model selected the correct command on every attempt. I classified that regression as absorbed rather than missed, excluding it from detector denominators while retaining it as a false-positive control. As expected, an arm where no operational failure occurred triggered zero behavioral alerts.

Detection results

Detector thresholds derived from the baseline runs:

  • Task success: Fires below 18 of 19 verified completions.
  • Token cost: Fires outside a ±37% volume envelope.
  • Tool calls: Fires outside a ±7% call count envelope.
  • Scope drift: Fires above a 0.135 threshold (calculated as 1 – overlap between the active task scopes and baseline scopes, averaged across all tasks).

Across the seven active regressions, tool-call counts and scope drift each caught four failures. Task success rates caught only two. Token costs flagged one, while the refund trap tasks caught zero.

Task success rates flagged only the two regressions that made task completion physically impossible. Swapping the model, modifying system prompts, failing 25% of network calls, serving stale data from replicas, and adding 1.5 seconds of API latency all left task completion steady at 18 or 19 out of 19.

The speed-pressure arm requires context: the agent completed every task using 21% fewer calls and 17% fewer tokens. Two behavioral detectors flagged this run because the execution pattern shifted significantly, even though the shift improved efficiency. Behavioral detectors report movement; engineering teams must decide if that movement represents progress or degradation.

How competent agents mask infrastructure faults

AI agents routinely mask underlying technical failures through three primary behaviors:

1. Automated retry logic

The flaky API arm absorbed all 31 injected network failures. Before retrying non-idempotent write operations, the agent queried the backend to confirm if the initial attempt had committed, preventing duplicate refunds. One task—a subscription cancellation followed by a customer notification—absorbed seven consecutive API failures during execution.

“As agent retry logic improves, downstream task completion becomes increasingly decoupled from infrastructure health.”

The arm verified 19 out of 19 tasks while executing 99 tool calls against the 58-call baseline. As agent retry logic improves, downstream task completion becomes increasingly decoupled from infrastructure health.

2. Autonomous workarounds

When provided with documentation for only 11 of 30 commands, the agent recovered missing endpoints by guessing plausible command names. It batched hundreds of experimental attempts into shell loops, distinguishing valid endpoints from invalid ones based on returned error structures.

Through this brute-force approach, the agent successfully discovered refund, messaging, file upload, search, and admin endpoints. It failed to discover subscription commands, causing six tasks to fail.

This recovery process consumed 161,013 tokens (73% above baseline) and took 15 minutes to execute, compared to the five-minute baseline. Because the agent executed these speculative loops locally, the attempts never hit the API audit log. The regression remained detectable almost entirely due to its extreme token overhead.

3. Caution under uncertainty

The stale-read arm highlights the limits of quantitative monitoring. All write operations committed successfully to the primary database, but 18 subsequent read operations fetched outdated state from the lagging replica.

When the agent closed a ticket and re-read its status, the record appeared open. When it processed an invoice refund and re-read the balance, the refund appeared unapplied.

Token usage increased by 22% (below the 37% alert threshold), tool calls increased by 5% (below the 7% threshold), and scope drift reached 0.133 (below the 0.135 threshold). Every quantitative metric remained completely green.

Stale Read Execution Flow:
Write to Primary (Success) ──► Read from Replica (Stale Data Returned)
│
▼
Agent Analyzes Discrepancy
│
▼
Agent Suppresses Retries & Logs Warning

However, the agent’s final text summary explicitly detailed the anomaly. It reported that none of its 19 writes could be verified via read-backs, systematically laid out the evidence for each task, and explained that it deliberately suppressed retries for refunds, comments, messages, and uploads to avoid double-applying mutations.

“Its defensive caution successfully contained the fault, but simultaneously rendered a severe infrastructure issue invisible to quantitative monitoring.”

Had the agent blindly retried those operations, it would have generated duplicate refunds and triggered production alerts. Its defensive caution successfully contained the fault, but simultaneously rendered a severe infrastructure issue invisible to quantitative monitoring. The sole indicator of failure existed inside the prose summary.

Token usage is a noisy metric

Token consumption was the single metric already tracked across every run, yet it proved almost useless for anomaly detection. Baseline token usage fluctuated by 18% across three identical runs, forcing a wide ±37% detection threshold. Consequently, the +26% token surge from the flaky API arm and the +36% surge from the model swap both slipped beneath the alert line undetected.

By contrast, tool-call volume varied by only 3% across the same baseline runs, enabling a tight ±7% detection threshold that easily flagged the 70% surge in API calls. Teams alerting on execution costs should track tool-call volume rather than raw token counts.

The degradation of adversarial test sets

Adversarial test cases measure specific vulnerabilities in specific model generations. The refund traps successfully differentiated model capabilities in September, but caught zero errors in October because every tested arm—including standalone runs on the smaller model—declined the unauthorized actions.

Two variables shifted between test runs: the underlying model updated, and the launch prompt wording changed slightly. (The September transcripts needed to reconstruct the exact original prompt were cleared from temporary storage before analysis.) However, isolated reruns conclusively ruled out queue positioning as a factor.

Recommended monitoring stack for production agents

To effectively monitor autonomous agents , track these four telemetry layers:

  • Log the resolved model ID on every run: Treat any shift in the returned model string as an active production deployment.
  • Track tool calls per verified task against a replicated baseline: Measure call volume alongside task completion. In the flaky API test, tool calls surged 70% above the 58-call baseline despite a stable 19/19 completion rate, surfacing 31 hidden transient errors.
  • Isolate transient errors and retry attempts into explicit metrics: Track retries directly; they’re an early-warning indicator of infrastructure degradation that the agent is actively paying to mask.
  • Parse final agent summaries for explicit statements of uncertainty: Treat final agent reports as structured telemetry rather than plain text output. In the stale-read test, the summary contained the only indicator of system failure.
  • Rotate adversarial test sets whenever the underlying model updates: Existing test suites measure the limitations of previous model iterations. When a model updates, update the adversarial evaluations accordingly.

Validating your monitoring controls

To evaluate your telemetry layer, execute your agent’s unmodified baseline three times across identical tasks and calculate two variance metrics: tokens per task and tool calls per task. Expect the tool-call variance to be significantly tighter than the token variance (my test runs yielded 3% and 18%, respectively).

Next, inject transient failures into 25% of upstream network calls and execute the suite again. If your agent is appropriately resilient, overall task completion will remain stable while total tool calls roughly double. If task completion drops immediately, the agent’s retry logic requires improvement.

Running this benchmark reveals which telemetry layers can detect production degradation—providing the visibility needed to catch silent failures before an unannounced model swap forces an investigation.

item.title: From open beta to global GA: What Docusign learned by bringing contract AI workflows to agents
item.description:
Connecting an AI agent to enterprise software is relatively easy. Making sure it can find the right information, carry out the intended task, and stay within a user’s permissions is where things get complicated.

That’s what Docusign discovered while developing its Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server, which entered open beta in May  2026 , and reached global general availability on September 30, 2026.

“There’s a big difference between building tools and solving actual customer problems.”

The Docusign MCP Server lets compatible AI assistants and agents access select Docusign capabilities to create, sign, and manage contracts without requiring users to switch applications. Someone could ask an assistant to find a contract, check its status, or prepare an agreement for signature, with Docusign handling the underlying work. A human remains ultimately responsible for reviewing and approving the transaction and its outcome.

“There’s a big difference between building tools and solving actual customer problems,” Sagnik Nandy , Docusign’s chief technology officer, tells The New Stack .

From APIs to AI agents

Traditional REST APIs let developers connect applications and automate tasks through predefined requests. AI agents work differently. A user describes what they want in natural language, and the agent works out which tools to use.

Docusign for Developers is a powerful suite of tools and resources designed to help developers build the solutions, workflows, and integrations their organizations and customers need across the entire agreement lifecycle.
Learn More

MCP is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to external data and tools. A server exposes capabilities that a connected AI application can discover and invoke.

Docusign wanted to make its Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM) platform available inside the AI tools their customers use, helping organizations create, commit to, and manage agreements. Through MCP, selected Docusign capabilities are accessible from the AI environments customers already use.

Docusign announced the open beta at its Momentum conference in New York in May 2026. Preparing it for wider use revealed challenges beyond the early demos.

What the beta revealed

Nandy says engineers working closely with customers can usually anticipate the prompts they’ll submit and the responses they expect. That gets harder when a wider audience has access to the same tools.

“Once you put it out there, you have to really get it right,” he says. “There are different kinds of prompts that come in. The different tools have to work together, both between themselves, but also across our tool boundary and the customer bringing in other tools.”

Feedback led Docusign to expand the contract data, workflow actions, and administrative controls  available through MCP.

“We added support for local files coming in, so a lot of people wanted to upload local data and interact based on that,” Nandy says.

That expanded access to information inside Docusign’s Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) software, the company’s most advanced set of contract-related capabilities built on the IAM platform for customers with the most complex agreement lifecycle needs and added support for local document uploads through the MCP Apps interface in supported clients. That lets users work with documents that are not already stored in Docusign, subject to the client and workflow support available.

“We also added account-level settings and options,” Nandy explains. “Adding support for people being able to do certain things or turn off certain things at that level, that was also useful.”

On September 4, 2026, Docusign announced plans for global availability, which its release notes confirm began on September 30. By GA, the server supported broader agreement workflows and AI-client connections, alongside account-level administration; local uploads use the MCP Apps interface where supported.

Docusign has also reported growing uptake. During its second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, the company said cumulative active accounts using MCP had more than quadrupled during the quarter, although it acknowledged that adoption was still in its early stages.

Reliability was another concern. In an October engineering account , Docusign described using guided interfaces, automated evaluations, and security testing to check how agents select and use its tools. Changes to an AI model or client can affect those interactions even when the underlying integration stays the same.

Keeping permissions intact

Giving external AI tools access to contract data raises security concerns, particularly when documents contain sensitive business information.

Nandy says Docusign uses OAuth 2.0 for authentication. Each tool call must have the required OAuth scopes and remain within the user’s Docusign permissions.

“There’s this fundamental principle that an MCP server strictly operates within the user’s Docusign permissions and authorization,” he explains. “So you should not be able to do anything that you wouldn’t be able to do in the product.”

The same restrictions apply when agents take action, while underlying API calls remain subject to Docusign’s existing logging and monitoring policies. These controls don’t govern how a third-party AI provider stores or uses data it receives; customers must also assess that provider’s data policies.

“Even though an agent is performing it, it doesn’t mean the agent should have any extra privileges.”

“Even though an agent is performing it, it doesn’t mean the agent should have any extra privileges,” Nandy says.

Account administrators can enable or disable MCP access for an account. Additional connector settings may vary by AI client. But permissions alone cannot prevent an agent from misunderstanding a request, so how it handles ambiguous instructions matters just as much.

One server, multiple AI clients

Docusign supports AI environments including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini Enterprise, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Slackbot, Salesforce Agentforce, and Perplexity.

The company maintains a shared MCP Server behind its client connectors, giving those integrations a common interface to Docusign contract data and agreement workflows..

“One of the design choices we made is we have a single MCP server, and the layer between our internal systems and MCP is pretty thin,” Nandy says.

“We also have a single MCP solution server as opposed to multiple specific to each client, which allows us to maintain consistency.”

Different AI clients may interpret requests or present information differently, and connectors may expose new tools at different times. The shared server gives Docusign a common place to maintain its capabilities and also supports custom agent integrations. Docusign recommends official connectors for production accounts and custom connectors for developer-account testing.

When an agent needs to ask questions

Someone might ask an agent to prepare an agreement without specifying which template to use, or request a document without saying whether they want the file or a link.

Nandy says Docusign has worked to support conversations where agents can ask for clarification instead of allowing an AI client to guess..

“One of the things we try to do is add support for user-guided feedback,” he says. “It can ask you questions like: Should you use a template for this? Or, if you want information back, do you want the entire file or a URL?”

That back-and-forth is one advantage of agent-based interactions over conventional API calls, where the application typically has to supply the required parameters.

“You can have these back-and-forth conversations. You can have that guided flow, and we leverage that strongly,” Nandy says.

For contract workflows, clarifying before acting could keep an agent from selecting the wrong document or proceeding with incomplete instructions. Guided MCP Apps provide structured steps in supported contract workflows, but the experience depends on the host’s capabilities.

MCP doesn’t replace APIs

Despite Docusign’s investment in MCP, Nandy doesn’t see it replacing traditional APIs. The company has long taken an API-first approach, and he argues that the choice depends on what developers are building.

“APIs often provide a certain level of determinism,” he says.

For processes with clearly defined inputs and outputs, a direct API call may make more sense. MCP helps when an agent needs to choose between tools as part of a broader request, though teams can use both approaches together.

“We’ve also seen solutions where both are used in tandem,” Nandy says, describing agents that can recognize when a single API endpoint handles a task better.

“APIs often provide a certain level of determinism.”

For engineering teams, the decision comes down to where an AI agent adds useful context or flexibility and where conventional automation already does the job.

Docusign’s move to general availability shows how much work sits behind an enterprise MCP integration for enterprise contract workflows. Supporting different AI clients is one challenge; making sure AI contract workflows behave reliably, respect permissions, and route ambiguity for clarification is another.

Developers can explore supported clients, authentication requirements, and available tools in Docusign’s MCP Server documentation .

item.title: How the new streamhouse architecture solves agentic AI’s data problem
item.description:
AI agents are moving from answering questions to taking action, and to do that effectively, they need to know the state of the business at any given moment. Most data architectures still aren’t designed to support querying subsecond updates across the enterprise, which is why the streamhouse has emerged to address this gap.

The streamhouse is a data architecture pattern that continuously delivers the current state of a business to applications and AI agents. A group of data infrastructure companies defined it to provide consistency around an approach many organizations have started to deploy independently anyway.

A streamhouse can be built from open-source technologies such as Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, and Apache Iceberg, from commercial products, or from a combination of both. The group behind it, which includes Confluent, Aiven, StreamNative and Ververica, has published an open, vendor-neutral definition at streamhouse.com , and anyone may use the name free of charge.

A common definition gives architects and data teams shorthand for what capabilities they need and where they sit relative to the rest of the stack. When a data engineer says “we need a streamhouse,” the CFO and other stakeholders can immediately understand what they mean and grasp the value.

A different kind of architecture

Most data architectures were designed to support business intelligence, where data is processed in batches for human analysis. The lakehouse does that job well and remains the right foundation for it. Agents need something different: data that reflects what’s happening now, delivered at machine speed.

Confluent, founded by the original creators of Apache Kafka, pioneered a complete data streaming platform that streams, connects, processes, and governs data as it flows throughout a business. With Confluent, any organization can modernize their business and run it in real-time.
Learn More
The latest from Confluent

“Agents need something different: data that reflects what’s happening now, delivered at machine speed.”

That calls for an architecture that continuously captures, processes, governs, and serves a real-time view of the business, so that applications and agents can act as events occur.

Use cases include order fulfillment, claims processing, underwriting, and fraud detection, all of which rely on real-time data from multiple sources. A claim might draw on policy records, payment history and customer interactions, and joining those sources as events happen is where the architecture is most valuable. Hyper-personalization in e-commerce and gaming are other examples.

What defines a streamhouse?

The open definition sets out three attributes. First, a streamhouse is real-time. Data stays current as events occur, rather than being refreshed on a batch schedule.

Second, it’s production-native. Analytical systems often lack the fault tolerance and service levels required for operational systems, because they were never intended to power the business. A streamhouse sits in the path of business-critical applications and agents, so it has to meet the same standard as those systems.

The third attribute is decentralization. A centralized model ingests data into one place and transforms it there, making it difficult and costly to reuse for anything besides analytics. A streamhouse transforms data to make it discoverable and contextualized, so that data produced once can be consumed many times by agents, applications, and dashboards alike.

Shaping data for AI

Freshness is one part of the problem, but data shape matters too. For decades, enterprises stored every fact exactly once in highly normalized relational tables. Storage was expensive, and normalization protected developers from update and deletion anomalies. As a result, many domain relationships are encoded in tables made up of little more than two foreign keys. That structure means very little to an AI model.

“…many domain relationships are encoded in tables made up of little more than two foreign keys. That structure means very little to an AI model.”

Consider an agent that drafts a follow-up email after a customer places an order. It needs to be certain that the customer lives at a particular address and just ordered a particular product, and it needs to know the moment the order is placed. Streaming captures those changes as events, enriches them with context, and delivers them to the agent in real time.

Delivering context in that structured, queryable form also limits how much extraneous information each model call needs, reducing costs.

Where the streamhouse fits

None of this makes the lakehouse obsolete. The two architectures will coexist in many organizations, and open table formats allow them to operate from a single, consistent view of data. The lakehouse is still the right place for historical analysis, reporting, and model training, where hours-old data is acceptable. The streamhouse handles the real-time, operational workloads the lakehouse was not designed to serve.

“With today’s ML models capable enough for most business tasks, the data agents act on will increasingly determine how well they perform.”

With today’s ML models capable enough for most business tasks, the data agents act on will increasingly determine how well they perform. For teams moving agents into production, a practical first step is to list the decisions those agents will make and identify where the data behind each one lives today. In most enterprises, that data is spread across several operational systems and reaches the analytics stack hours later. A streamhouse is designed to close that gap.

item.title: Dropbox ditched AWS S3 for its own in-house system. Now it’s buying Tigris to sell S3-compatible storage to AI developers.
item.description:
Dropbox is entering the AI infrastructure space in a big way, announcing plans on Thursday to acquire Tigris , a startup that provides object storage for AI applications.

The cloud-storage giant tells The New Stack that it’s paying $350 million for Tigris, a move designed to accelerate Dropbox’s own ambitions in selling storage infrastructure to developers and businesses. Indeed, alongside the acquisition news, Dropbox also announced DBX Agent Cloud, an upcoming offering that will initially let developers purchase object storage directly from Dropbox.

Dropbox, it’s worth noting, is no stranger to building storage infrastructure itself. Kicking off in 2015, the company moved more than 90% of its user data off Amazon’s S3 cloud storage service onto an in-house system dubbed Magic Pocket , in a bid to improve performance and reduce costs. But as Dropbox chief business officer Eric Webster explains, selling storage infrastructure to external customers presents an entirely different set of challenges.

“Operating infrastructure for Dropbox and offering a storage product to developers involve different requirements,” Webster tells The New Stack . “Tigris brings a working commercial product, an experienced team, developer relationships and early customer traction.”

“Tigris brings a working commercial product, an experienced team, developer relationships and early customer traction.”

That “customer traction” includes a slew of companies such as Amplified, Railway, Runpod, and Replicate, spanning everything from developer hosting platforms to GPU infrastructure and AI model deployment. Precisely the kinds of businesses that need fast, reliable access to large volumes of data, often while running applications and AI models across different environments.

Eye of the Tigris

Founded in 2022 by former Uber engineers Ovais Tariq (CEO), Himank Chaudhary (CTO), and chief architect Yevgeniy Firsov , Tigris has built an S3-compatible storage platform that allows developers to keep their data accessible across different cloud and compute environments.

For developers training AI models, that could mean storing large datasets in one place while renting computing power from multiple providers. Using Amazon S3 in such situations can incur additional data-transfer costs, known as egress fees, and delays, particularly when the computing happens outside AWS. Tigris addresses this by automatically keeping data close to where it’s needed, while charging no egress fees for transfers out of its storage service.

The company announced a $25 million Series A round of funding in October 2025, with investors including Spark Capital and existing backer Andreessen Horowitz.

While much of Tigris’s appeal lies in its existing product, customers and developer relationships, Dropbox sees an opportunity to turn that foothold into a much bigger business in the commercial storage infrastructure market.

“Combining those strengths with Dropbox’s experience operating storage at scale would give us a faster path into this market,” Webster says. “The acquisition lets us build on what both teams have already developed and learned from their customers.”

And so one of the clearest expressions of that ambition is DBX Agent Cloud, a service through which Dropbox plans to sell storage infrastructure to developers building AI applications, with Tigris expected to provide the underlying object-storage technology if the acquisition passes the usual array of regulatory approvals.

But why is Dropbox making this push into AI infrastructure? And why now?

“AI applications are creating and working with growing volumes of content, from images and video to training datasets and model artifacts,” Webster says. “As models and compute providers change, that content needs a consistent home.”

“AI applications are creating and working with growing volumes of content, from images and video to training datasets and model artifacts.”

Founded in 2007, Dropbox has spent the best part of two decades dealing with the challenges of storing and managing vast amounts of customer data, from consumers through the enterprise. And it now hopes to put that experience to work for developers building their own applications.

“DBX Agent Cloud extends that expertise to companies and developers building applications, starting with standalone object storage,” Webster says.

The plan, ultimately, is to add filesystem and content-processing capabilities next, allowing AI applications to work with different types of content, track files, and pick up where they left off across sessions.

Dropbox has yet to provide a launch date for DBX Agent Cloud, or explain exactly how the two companies’ technologies will be integrated.

“We’ll share more about the technical integration and availability as those plans develop,” Webster says.

As for existing Tigris customers, well, Dropbox is promising business as usual, at least initially. Webster says they won’t “need to migrate or change how they use the service” when the acquisition closes, and will “continue to receive support for the Tigris product.”

What happens further down the line is less certain, particularly as Dropbox builds out its own filesystem and content-processing capabilities around Tigris’s foundation.

“As the product evolves, we’ll communicate directly with customers before any changes that affect them,” Webster adds.

Dropbox puts AI to work on files

Alongside the acquisition news on Thursday, Dropbox also announced what it’s calling a “major evolution” of its main product, one that “brings AI-powered capabilities directly to customers’ existing files and workflows,” the company says.

Back in 2023, Dropbox debuted Dash , an AI-powered search tool that allowed users to find information scattered across services such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Dropbox itself. Now, the company is taking things further, allowing users to instruct AI to work directly on their files, from editing PDFs and images, to reorganising folders, transcribing recordings, and completing multi-step tasks.

“Customers told us they wanted these AI-powered features directly in the product where their content and workflows already live,” Mike Torres , Dropbox’s chief product officer, tells The New Stack .

The company had already begun integrating Dash into Dropbox last year, bringing AI-powered search, document summaries, and the ability to ask questions about stored content into the core product.

“The new experience builds on that foundation and what we’ve learned from customers, helping them move from finding and understanding information to organizing files, editing content, and completing supported multi-step tasks,” Torres continues.

“We want customers to have the freedom to use the AI tools that work best for them.”

Dropbox says more than 70,000 teams have received access to the new capabilities, although it hasn’t disclosed how many are actively using them. As for pricing, Torres says that eligible Standard and Advanced plans include a certain allocation of AI credits, with customers able to purchase more as needed.

The company is also giving users a choice of AI models within Dropbox, alongside integrations with third-party tools including ChatGPT and Claude. These connections allow customers to work with their Dropbox files through external AI services without repeatedly uploading them, with the resulting content saved back to Dropbox.

“We want customers to have the freedom to use the AI tools that work best for them,” Torres says.

Behind that, perhaps, lies a similar philosophy to the Tigris acquisition: allowing developers to choose where they run their AI applications while keeping the underlying data accessible. Dropbox is betting it can turn that proposition into a substantial new infrastructure business, although with no launch date yet for DBX Agent Cloud, it remains to be seen how that ambition will translate into reality.

item.title: Postgres and ClickHouse can share tables. EnterpriseDB wants one set of rules to govern them.
item.description:
If you have built anything that needs both a system of record and fast analytics , you know the shape of the problem. Postgres ® holds the orders, the accounts, the state your application cannot afford to get wrong. ClickHouse software answers the questions.

A row store tuned for transactions was never built to answer at speed: what happened across a billion events in the last hour, which cohort is churning, what the agent should do next. Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The misery lives entirely in the gap between them.

“Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The misery lives entirely in the gap between them.”

EnterpriseDB (EDB) has acquired Altinity, the independent company behind Altinity Stable Builds, the Altinity Kubernetes Operator, and Altinity.Cloud.

The headline is corporate. The reason a developer should care is narrower: The #1 contributor to Postgres and the people who have run ClickHouse software in production for nearly a decade now work on one roadmap, and that roadmap is aimed at three pains you live with every week.

Pain 1: The CDC job is the product nobody asked for

Count the moving parts between a committed Postgres transaction and the same row being queryable in ClickHouse software. A replication slot. A connector with its own failure modes. A message broker you size, secure, and patch. A sink that must survive schema changes without silently dropping columns. A dedup strategy, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates.

EDB Postgres® AI (PG AI) is the sovereign AI data system for the agentic enterprise. It unifies transactional, analytical, and AI workloads in a single architecture, with governance enforced at the data layer and the flexibility to deploy on-premises, in hybrid environments, or across clouds.
Learn More
The latest from EnterpriseDB

Monitoring on every hop, because lag in any one of them turns a “real-time” dashboard into a lie. None of that code is your product. All of it is on your on-call rota, and it is the reason the page comes at 3 a.m.

Pain 2: Your agent is reasoning over last night’s data

Agentic workloads changed the economics of staleness. A dashboard 20 minutes behind is annoying. An agent that approves a refund, reprices inventory, or flags a transaction on a 20-minute-old aggregate is wrong, and wrong at machine speed, thousands of times before anyone notices.

“An agent that approves a refund, reprices inventory, or flags a transaction on a 20-minute-old aggregate is wrong, and wrong at machine speed…”

So developers building agents write the same awkward code: Query Postgres for current state, query ClickHouse software for the trend, stitch the two in the application, and hope the clocks agree. You have become the integration layer, and the integration layer is where the bugs live.

Pain 3: You run the stack twice

Every row-level rule, masked column, and “analysts see aggregates, not customer IDs” policy exists once in Postgres and again in ClickHouse software, and the two drift the first time someone updates one and forgets the other. Operating ClickHouse software on Kubernetes is its own job: Keeper, storage classes, replica placement, backups, upgrades, and one or two engineers who have quietly become “the ClickHouse people.”

And if you took the shortcut of a managed analytics service, your data lives where the vendor says and your bill scales with their pricing model, not with your infrastructure. Two engines, two permission models, two operators, two support contracts, and a lock-in you did not choose.

Read against those three pains, the deal starts to make sense: Each one maps to a pillar of what EDB and Altinity now plan to build together.

Pillar 1: One shared layer, not a pipeline

Today, Postgres, WarehousePG (EDB’s MPP warehouse), and ClickHouse software can read the same Apache Iceberg tables and query each other. Postgres writes the record and ClickHouse software reads it through the same open table format, with less data movement and integration effort between them. What is planned is one shared catalog and one governance model across all three engines, and one sovereign control plane for Postgres and ClickHouse software.

The organizing architecture is Iceberg as the shared layer today, with EDB’s control plane to follow as the shared operation. Treat the shared catalog as what is being built, not what you can download today. But the design goal is the one you would set yourself: fewer hops, one catalog, no bespoke reconciliation code. The CDC job is meant to stop being something you own.

Pillar 2: Live data for agents, governed where it lives

EDB Postgres AI pairs a sovereign multi-model data layer with an agentic runtime and governance enforced in Postgres at the data layer—at the point of action and with an audit trail. For an agent, the goal is that it asks for business context and gets the record and the analysis from one system, rather than your code orchestrating two databases and a queue.

For permissions, one governance model across all three engines is part of the plan. Today, Postgres enforces purpose-bound access for agents, and ClickHouse software enforces its own role-based access. The plan is to define the policy once, where the data lives, and let every engine enforce it instead of re-implementing it in application code or a second permission model. That allows your agents to reason over what is true now without the security review blocking your release.

Pillar 3: The operators, the experts, and the choice of where it runs

Altinity’s answer to running ClickHouse software in production has been the Kubernetes Operator , with more than 100 million pulls, and Altinity Stable Builds maintained for three years with security and bug-fix backports. That knowledge now sits inside the #1 contributor to Postgres, which also created CloudNativePG and donated it to the open source community, where it is now a CNCF project and the Postgres operator many teams already run. One vendor understands both operators.

The plan is one sovereign control plane that runs Postgres and ClickHouse software, with one support organization behind it on the night they interact badly. Where it runs is yours to decide: bring-your-own-cloud, self-hosted on your own Kubernetes or OpenShift, air-gapped, or fully managed. Altinity.Cloud already deploys into customers’ own cloud accounts, and EDB Postgres AI runs in your own account or on-premises. So if your regulator, your CFO, or your latency budget says the data stays here, the stack follows you rather than the other way round.

The one answer

Three pains, three pillars, one conclusion: The application layer should stop being the place where two databases are reconciled. Postgres keeps the record. ClickHouse software answers the hard questions on the same live data. Everything you delete from the middle is code you no longer debug, monitor, or explain to an auditor.

“The best pipeline is the one you never have to write.”

The best pipeline is the one you never have to write. For developers who have spent years keeping two databases in agreement by hand and explaining the drift to auditors, product managers, and themselves, that is the promise worth watching. And it is the first thing to test as each planned piece lands.
